title: Astrometry of 3I/ATLAS before perihelion predicts its 2026 path with an r^-2 force, not a water-ice law; after perihelion small-telescope positions are 900 km tailward; A1 varies 2x
abstract: We fit the orbit of the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS to 8,442 MPC positions (2025-05-08 to 2026-04-14) with ASSIST/DE440 and Marsden A1-A3 terms. Positions before 2025-10-01 already need a radial acceleration with g = (1 au/r)^2: A1 = 5.7 +- 1.8 x 10^-8 au/d^2 (delta chi2 = 9, formal weights). This pre-perihelion model predicts the positions of Feb-Apr 2026 to 0.7-1.6 arcsec, where gravity only misses by 11-12 arcsec. It misses by 4-6 arcsec in Nov 2025-Jan 2026, which is more than its forecast width. The water-ice g(r) law misses by 47-62 arcsec. Small-telescope positions differ from large-telescope (1.5 m or larger, HST) positions in the same 3-day bins. After perihelion, a 3-D tailward photocentre offset of 907 +- 122 km, scaled by the phase angle, fits these differences better than a timing offset. Before perihelion, the apparent motion was within about 5 degrees of the Sun line, so a 3.1 s lead along the motion and a sunward offset cannot be separated. For one r^-2 law, A1 is 2.9 to 6.2 x 10^-8 au/d^2, depending on the data selection and the offset model. The formal errors are 0.07-0.6. Large telescopes alone give A1 = 5.5 +- 0.6, A2 = 2.1 +- 0.5 and A3 = -0.67 +- 0.04, which agree with Spada et al. (2026). A common sunward offset of K (1000 km) in the large-telescope positions changes A1 by -0.87 K, and the astrometry constrains K only weakly. Limitations: we do not know the absolute offset of the large telescopes, we define the classes by station name, our weights are simple, we do not model a time-delayed g(r), and we have no positions after 2026-04-14.

display.caption: Orbits fit to positions before 2025-10-01 compared with later positions (weekly median O-C; dots = large telescopes). An r^-2 radial term (blue) predicts the 2026 path; gravity only (grey) and the water-ice law (red) do not.

Small-telescope minus large-telescope positions in 3-day bins, in the Sun-line frame (top) and in the apparent-motion frame (middle), with phase angle and apparent rate (bottom). After perihelion, the offset is tailward and follows the phase angle.

Fitted A1, A2, A3 (g = (1 au/r)^2) for different data selections, weights and offset models, compared with Spada et al. (2026) and JPL #55. A1 changes by a factor of 2; the formal errors are much smaller.

citations.reason: We adapted its ASSIST orbit fitter (orbfit.py), its MPC data recipe and its weighting and debiasing scheme.

Spada, Krolikowska and Dones 2026: systematic and statistical uncertainties of the 3I/ATLAS non-gravitational acceleration. Our large-telescope A1-A3 agree with their full-arc ng1 values, and we also find a pre/post-perihelion mismatch. We add an explicit class-offset model and a forecast test.
JPL SBDB orbit #55 (2026-10-21) and Horizons vectors; starting state and residual comparison.
MPC ADES astrometry of 3I (8,442 optical positions) and observatory codes.
JPL planetary and lunar ephemerides DE440 and DE441 (Park et al. 2021).
Eggl et al. 2020 star-catalogue debiasing of optical astrometry.
Marsden, Sekanina and Yeomans 1973 non-gravitational force model and water-ice g(r).
Cordiner et al. 2025: JWST detection of a CO2-dominated coma of 3I/ATLAS at 3.32 au; context for the r^-2 activity law before perihelion.
Thoss et al. 2026: mass and size of 3I/ATLAS from its non-gravitational acceleration; our A1 range propagates into such estimates.
Forbes and Butler 2025: size of 3I/ATLAS from non-gravitational acceleration.
HST nucleus and post-perihelion activity of 3I/ATLAS (nucleus radius 1.3 +- 0.2 km).
